appraisal_events.evidence: Monsieur a une facilité de parole, une mémoire !... comme j'en ai rarement rencontré... on peut dire qu'avec M. Bréchot, vous avez là deux numéros qui se valent, je ne sais même pas si...celui-ci ne damerait pas encore le pion au professeur. Ça vient plus naturellement, c'est moins recherché.
appraisal_events.explanation: Forcheville lavishly praises the painter's fluency and memory in quoted speech, comparing him favorably to Brichot the professor and suggesting his natural eloquence may even surpass Brichot's more studied manner.

appraisal_events.evidence: Mme Verdurin... avait soudain dépouillé son visage de toute vie, de toute motilité... Ce n'était plus qu'une cire perdue, qu'un masque de plâtre... une majesté presque papale... Mais le marbre finit par s'animer et fit entendre qu'il fallait ne pas être dégoûté pour aller chez ces gens-là, car la femme était toujours ivre et le mari si ignorant qu'il disait collidor pour corridor. — On me paierait bien cher que je ne laisserais pas entrer ça chez moi, conclut Mme Verdurin, en regardant Swann d'un air impérieux.
appraisal_events.explanation: After Forcheville names Swann's aristocratic connections (La Trémoïlle, les Laumes), the narrator mock-heroically inflates Mme Verdurin's theatrical deafness into statuary grandeur before deflating it with her coarse dismissal of those same aristocrats, exposing her performed indifference as petty, possessive snobbery; she closes by staring imperiously at Swann as she declares she would never admit 'ça' to her house.

status_effects.explanation: The painter's conversational eloquence is elevated by Forcheville's enthusiastic, extended praise, which places him on par with or above Brichot as a talker.
The narrator's ironic, statue-and-marble imagery exposes her elaborate pretense of not having heard the aristocratic names as defensive, possessive posturing rather than genuine indifference.

Though the mention of his high-society connections is noted as inaccurate, it provokes the clan's reproving silence, and Mme Verdurin's closing imperious look at Swann signals that his standing with the little clan is being asserted over and watched.

ambiguities: "M. Bréchot" in Forcheville's speech is resolved to the reference sheet's Brichot, but the garbled spelling leaves some uncertainty about whether this is simply Forcheville's careless pronunciation or a distinct rendering.

Swann's own reaction to Mme Verdurin's declaration and imperious look is not shown in the passage, so the social-status effect on him is inferred from her gesture and tone rather than from any depicted response.
